summary.text: A 42-year-old man with hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus and hyperlipidemia presented with shortness of breath on exertion, progressive lower limb swelling extending to his knees and loss of appetite, with cough and shortness of breath beginning a month earlier. He had previously consumed high amounts of alcohol, denied smoking or illicit drugs, and was dyspneic, tachycardic, with jugular venous distention and 3+ lower extremity edema.

He was in cardiogenic shock, and work-up showed a severely dilated left ventricle with severe systolic dysfunction and massive thrombi in the RV and LV apices on echocardiography, a large infarct on stress PET, multiple pulmonary emboli with lung infarcts and a right pleural effusion on CT angiography, and occlusion of the right common femoral artery. Cardiac MRI showed an LVEF of 15 % with nonviable myocardium in half of the LV. The hypercoagulable and cancer work-up was unremarkable.

He was transferred to the cardiac intensive care unit and started on furosemide and a heparin drip. Given minimal expected myocardial recovery, a multidisciplinary committee chose VA-ECMO as a bridge to orthotopic heart transplantation, and he was listed UNOS status 1 by exception. Four days after VA-ECMO he underwent transplantation; the explanted heart showed extensive biventricular thrombosis and scarring consistent with ischemic cardiomyopathy.

Six days after transplantation he developed RV dysfunction needing inotropic support and a pericardial effusion; biopsy suggested grade 2R acute cellular rejection and he received methylprednisolone, a steroid taper and tacrolimus, mycophenolate and prednisone. He was weaned off inotropes, a repeat biopsy showed resolution of rejection, and he was discharged home on direct oral anticoagulants 20 days after transplantation and will require close follow-up.
